title: Banda's end
hook: Banda is tortured and killed in Delhi, with his young son

segments.voice: Yesterday, the captives in Delhi, offered their lives if they would give up their faith. Your line was none renounced. Where did you say plainly what matters to you? Today the story of Banda Singh reaches its last day. Go gently. Day eight hundred forty-six.

A cot by a river at Nanded. A hermit hurries home, finds a stranger sitting where no one sits, and ends the day calling himself that stranger's banda, his servant. It was only nine days ago on this path. In the story it's years. The servant carried five arrows north, took towns, struck coins in his Gurus' names, gave fields to farmers, ran through the hills, starved behind mud walls, and was marched in chains to Delhi. Now his companions are gone, and his own turn has come. Today: Banda's end.
screen: `A COT BY A RIVER AT NANDED.` → `FROM SERVANT TO PRISONER.` → `HIS OWN TURN COMES.`

segments.voice: Sikh tellings of Banda Singh's last day are hard, and they don't need to be told in full to be understood. He was brought out in Delhi with his young son, Ajai Singh. Tradition says he was offered his life, as the others were, if he would give up his faith, and he refused. Then the hardest part of the telling. Tradition says his little boy was killed in front of him, and that Banda Singh did not break. Then he himself was put to death, slowly, by torture. The tellings dwell less on the pain than on his stillness. Some say an official asked him how a man who had done so much could come to this, and that he answered calmly, speaking of God's will and of how wrongdoers are punished in God's time. The exact words vary, and it's best not to put new ones in his mouth. That's the carry: he did not break. Not that he wasn't hurt. Not that he wasn't afraid. Only that what he'd chosen at that cot by the river stayed chosen to the end. Sikhs remember him by the fuller name, Banda Singh Bahadur, the brave. They remember him in more than one way, too; parts of his story were argued over by Sikhs who came after, and that's a story for tomorrow. But on this day, the memory is simple. The man who began by calling himself a servant ended as one, keeping faith with the One he served.
screen: `BROUGHT OUT WITH HIS YOUNG SON.` · `OFFERED HIS LIFE, HE REFUSES.` · `THE TELLINGS DWELL ON HIS STILLNESS.` · `A SERVANT TO THE END.` · then, large: `HE DID NOT BREAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a lamp for the brave. If you have a candle, a lamp, or even a phone light, turn it on and set it in front of you. If not, picture a small flame. Sit, and let the breath slow. Look at the light without staring. Let it stand for the people who didn't break: Banda Singh, his son, the captives in Delhi, and anyone you know of, in any time, who kept faith under pressure. You don't need words. Let the light do the remembering. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Banda's end. The death of Banda Singh Bahadur in Delhi, with his young son, when, tradition says, he refused to give up his faith and did not break. Today's word.
Your line: he did not break. Today, when something presses on you, take one slow breath before you answer it, and stay who you chose to be. Day eight hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur's death in Delhi, with his young son Ajai Singh, as a martyrdom, and honor him by the name Bahadur, the brave.

notes: Audit: 'the name later generations gave him' (Bahadur) was unsourced, since some tellings date the title to his lifetime; now 'the fuller name'. The review's 'offered their lives for their faith' read as if they volunteered; now 'offered their lives if they would give up their faith'.
Editor: changed the hook opener so it no longer repeats day 840's 'Go back', and replaced the narrator's superlative 'the cruelest part'.
The son's name Ajai Singh and his being killed before his father follow common Sikh tellings; graphic details deliberately left out. Confirm.
The official's question and Banda Singh's answer (God's will, punishment of wrongdoers) are paraphrased loosely and flagged as varying; a Keeper may prefer to cut it.
'Parts of his story were argued over by Sikhs who came after' sets up day 847 (the Tat Khalsa / Bandai split) without teaching it; confirm framing.
'It was only nine days ago on this path' refers to day 837; this is a count of days on the path itself, not a historical claim.
